chapter.name: Electoral Reforms
chapter.blurb: Committees on electoral reform and the reforms before 1996, of 1996, after 1996 and since 2010, including NOTA, VVPAT, convicted legislators, party funding and the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021.

concepts.name: Committees and commissions on electoral reform
concepts.description: The fourteen committees and commissions the chapter lists, who headed or appointed them, what each studied and when, and the four heads under which the resulting reforms are grouped.
concepts.idea: The chapter lists fourteen bodies from the 1971-72 Joint Parliamentary Committee to the Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) whose recommendations produced the reforms.
concepts.rule: The list begins with the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Amendments to Election Laws (1971-72) and the unofficial Tarkunde Committee, appointed by Jaya Prakash Narayan in 1974 during his Total Revolution movement, which reported in 1975 (p.825). The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) was appointed by the V.P. Singh Government when Goswami was Law Minister, and some of its recommendations were implemented in 1996 (pp.825-826). The Vohra Committee (1993) examined the nexus between crime and politics, and the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998), appointed by the BJP-led Government and reporting in 1999, upheld state funding of elections (pp.825, 833). Other entries are the Election Commission's recommendations (1998) and report (2004), the Law Commission's 170th (1999), 244th (2014) and 255th (2015) reports, the Venkatachaliah commission (2000-2002), the Second ARC report headed by Veerappa Moily (2007), the Tankha Core Committee (2010) and the J.S. Verma report on criminal law (2013) (p.825). The reforms are studied under four heads: before 1996, of 1996, after 1996 and since 2010 (p.825).
concepts.example: A question that asks which committee dealt with state funding of elections is answered by the Indrajit Gupta Committee, not by the Dinesh Goswami or Vohra committees (pp.825, 833).

concepts.name: Electoral reforms before 1996 and of 1996
concepts.description: The 1988-89 reforms (voting age, deputation, proposers, EVMs, booth capturing), the 1993 photo identity cards and the 1996 package drawn from the Dinesh Goswami Committee.
concepts.idea: The pre-1996 steps lowered the voting age and tightened rolls and polling, and the 1996 Act enacted Goswami's proposals on listing, nominations, polling-day rules and by-elections.
concepts.rule: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, and a 1989 Act placed roll staff on deputation to the Election Commission, set proposers for Rajya Sabha and council polls at 10 per cent of electors or ten, whichever is less, enabled EVMs and provided for adjourning or countermanding polls for booth capturing (p.826). The Election Commission decided in 1993 to issue photo identity cards to check bogus voting and impersonation (p.826). The 1996 reforms list candidates in three categories in alphabetical order, disqualify for six years those convicted under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, ban liquor for 48 hours before the close of poll, and require ten proposers for a candidate not sponsored by a recognised party and one for a recognised party's candidate (pp.826-827). They also stop countermanding on a candidate's death with, as the chapter puts it, a seven-day option for a recognised party (current practice countermands the poll when a recognised party's candidate dies, which lies outside the chapter), require by-elections within six months with two exceptions, give a paid holiday on polling day, limit candidates to two constituencies, make arms near polling stations a cognizable offence and cut the campaign gap from 20 to 14 days (pp.827-828).
concepts.example: A candidate of a registered-unrecognised party needs ten registered electors as proposers, while a recognised party's candidate needs one (p.827).

concepts.idea: Between 1997 and 2009 the reforms widened voting facilities, forced candidates to disclose antecedents and changed how Rajya Sabha elections are held.
concepts.rule: In 1997 the proposers and seconders for the President rose from 10 to 50 and for the Vice-President from 5 to 20, and the deposit for both went from Rs 2,500 to Rs 15,000 (p.828). In 1998 staff of local authorities, nationalised banks, universities, LIC, government undertakings and aided institutions became available for election duty, in 1999 notified classes could vote by postal ballot only, and in 2003 service voters of the Armed Forces could opt for proxy voting (p.828). A 2003 Commission order made candidates declare convictions, pending serious cases, assets of self, spouse and dependents, liabilities and education, and false information is an electoral offence (p.828). In 2003 the Rajya Sabha domicile requirement was removed and an open ballot, shown to the party's nominated agent, replaced the secret ballot to curb cross-voting and money power; travel of campaigning leaders is exempt from candidate expenses, rolls are supplied free to recognised-party candidates and electronic media time is shared equitably (p.829). Braille signage was tried at Asifnagar in 2004, in Delhi in 2008 and used in the 2009 Lok Sabha elections (p.829).
concepts.example: A Rajya Sabha elector who belongs to a party must show the marked ballot to the party's nominated agent (p.829).

concepts.idea: The 2009-2013 amendments tightened election procedure on exit polls, deposits, disqualification and roll appeals and widened enrolment.
concepts.rule: The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2009, effective 1 February 2010, bars conducting and publicising exit polls during the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections for the period the Election Commission notifies (pp.829-830, 834). It fixed a three-month limit for sending a corrupt practice case to the President, brought all officials appointed or deputed by the Commission within the corrupt practice of obtaining assistance and raised deposits to Rs 25,000 and Rs 12,500 (Lok Sabha) and Rs 10,000 and Rs 5,000 (assembly) for general and SC/ST candidates (p.830). Appeals against Electoral Registration Officers now go to the District Magistrate or equivalent and further to the state's Chief Electoral Officer (p.830). In 2010 citizens living abroad who have not acquired another citizenship became entitled to register in the constituency of their passport residence, and in 2013 online filing of enrolment applications was provided through the Registration of the Electors (Amendment) Rules, 2013 (p.830).

concepts.name: Reforms of 2013-2015: NOTA, VVPAT, convicted legislators and photographs
concepts.description: NOTA and the VVPAT (Supreme Court directions and permission), the jail-contest ruling and Parliament's response, the Lily Thomas ruling on Section 8(4) and the Election Commission's photograph order.
concepts.idea: Rulings of 2013 led to NOTA and VVPAT, Parliament reversed the jail-contest ruling but withdrew its Bill against the convicted-legislators ruling, and an Election Commission order added candidates' photographs.
concepts.rule: On the Supreme Court's directions the Commission provided a NOTA option from the 2013 assembly elections, continued in 2014; if NOTA votes exceed those of any candidate the candidate with the most votes is declared elected (pp.830-831). The VVPAT is an independent system attached to the EVM; its slip is visible for seven seconds, then falls into a sealed dropbox, the law was amended in 2013, the Court allowed phased introduction as an 'indispensable requirement', and it was first used at Noksen, Nagaland in 2013 (p.831). In 2013 the Court upheld a Patna High Court order that a person in jail or police custody cannot contest, and Parliament amended the Representation of the People Act, 1951 so that such a person remains an elector and a legislator is disqualified only under the Act (p.831). In Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013) the Court struck down Section 8(4) and made disqualification of convicted MPs and MLAs immediate; the Bill to nullify it was withdrawn (p.831). For elections after 1 May 2015, ballot papers and EVMs carry the candidate's picture, name and symbol, and a missing photo is no ground to reject nomination (p.832).
concepts.example: A voter in an assembly election in 2013 could press NOTA to reject every candidate; the leading candidate would still be declared elected (pp.830-831).

concepts.idea: The chapter records party funding rules being relaxed and re-routed between 2003 and 2018, and the 2021 Act linking rolls with Aadhaar and widening enrolment dates and premises.
concepts.rule: In 2003 parties were allowed to accept any amount from any person or company other than a government company, with contributions above Rs 20,000 reported to the Commission for income tax relief and companies given income tax exemption (p.829). The 2017 budget lowered the anonymous cash donation limit from Rs 20,000 to Rs 2,000 and removed the 7.5 per cent of net profit cap on corporate contributions and the duty to report them in the profit and loss account (p.832). The chapter describes the Electoral Bond Scheme notified in 2018 as a bearer instrument without the buyer's name, bought by citizens or Indian entities in denominations from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1 crore, usable for donations to registered parties with at least one per cent of votes and encashed through an authorised bank account, with buyer details confidential except to courts or in criminal cases (p.832). The 2018 budget allowed foreign funds to parties by amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (p.833). The Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 enabled Aadhaar linking, specified four qualifying dates, allowed spouses of service voters to vote in person or by post and expanded requisition of premises (p.833). Outside the chapter: the Electoral Bond Scheme and the removal of the corporate-donation cap and of the duty to report such donations were struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024, and the chapter pre-dates that ruling; the items therefore state these only as the chapter's account.
concepts.example: A donor giving a party Rs 5,000 in anonymous cash would exceed the Rs 2,000 limit the chapter describes after the 2017 budget (p.832).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The 2018 Union Budget allowed political parties to receive funds from foreign companies.
Statement-II: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 was accordingly amended and the definition of a foreign company modified.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: the 2018 Budget allowed political parties to receive funds from foreign companies; this describes the amendment, not the full scope of foreign-contribution law today. Statement-II is correct: the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 was amended and the definition of a foreign company modified. Statement-II explains Statement-I: amending the Act and the definition was the way the permission was given effect.
w: Rejected: Statement-II does explain Statement-I: the amendment of the Act and the definition of a foreign company was how the permission was given effect.
Rejected: Statement-II is correct, since the Act and the definition of a foreign company were amended.
Rejected: Statement-I is correct, since the 2018 Budget allowed such funding.
